171.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
171.explanation: Guru Nanak tells both communities of his day that taking what belongs to someone else is as forbidden as their strongest dietary taboo.
171.tie_back: The Kural says that giving up fairness and setting one's heart on another's property brings ruin and guilt at once; Guru Nanak makes another person's rightful due the most forbidden thing of all.
171.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
171._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the wrong of taking another's rightful due; the Kural condemns even the desire, while the verse targets the taking, and the ruin of the family is not mentioned.

172.explanation: In a salok of Ramkali ki Vaar, Guru Nanak condemns those who sit in judgment and make a show of piety, but sell justice for a bribe.
172.tie_back: The Kural says those who feel shame at unfairness will never do disgraceful things for gain; Guru Nanak shows the shameless opposite, people who trade fairness for a bribe.
172.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 951, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
172._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit by contrast: fairness sold for gain is exactly what the Kural's sense of shame prevents, but the verse names the vice rather than the virtue of shame.

173.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false.”
173.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that sensual enjoyments pursued for their own sake lead to ruin, while the true joy lies in the Lord's Name.
173.tie_back: The Kural says those who seek the lasting joy will not do wrong for a small passing pleasure; Guru Nanak likewise calls such pleasures false compared with lasting delight in God.
173.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
173._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the contrast between false, passing pleasures and true joy is shared, but the verse does not tie that contrast to coveting other people's goods.

174.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you see someone else's buttered bread, do not envy him for it.”
174.explanation: In this salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi Sheikh Farid tells the person of plain means to be content with simple fare and not to hanker after the richer bread on another's plate.
174.tie_back: The Kural says the self-mastered will not covet others' goods even when they think, we are poor; Farid gives the same counsel to the poor man looking at a richer table.
174.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 29 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
174._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: poverty is no excuse for coveting another's goods; Farid was a Muslim Sufi whose saloks are part of Sikh scripture, so this is Sikh canon though not by a Guru.

175.quote_or_event: “If an educated person is a sinner, then the illiterate holy man is not to be punished.”
175.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak teaches that learning does not save a person who does wrong, while a simple person who lives rightly does not suffer for lacking it.
175.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a sharp and wide mind is if its owner covets and acts senselessly; Guru Nanak likewise holds that learning is worth nothing without right conduct.
175.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
175._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: learning without conduct counts for nothing in both, but the verse speaks of sin in general, not coveting in particular.

176.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak mocks officials who devour people through bribery and oppression while still keeping up the forms of prayer and piety.
176.tie_back: The Kural warns that even one who has stood on the path of virtue is ruined once he covets others' wealth and plots to get it; Guru Nanak shows such outward piety emptied by greed.
176.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
176._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse attacks hypocrites who were never sincere, whereas the Kural describes a genuinely virtuous person falling; in Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak criticizes the hypocrisy of Hindu officials as well, so it is not aimed at Muslims alone.

177.quote_or_event: “For the sake of this wealth, so many were ruined; because of this wealth, so many have been disgraced.”
177.explanation: In a hymn on the devastation of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak reflects that wealth gathered and fought over has brought ruin and disgrace on many.
177.tie_back: The Kural warns that prosperity won by coveting rarely bears good fruit when it ripens; Guru Nanak shows that harvest of ruin and disgrace.
177.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
177._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on the bitter fruit of grasping wealth; the verse speaks of wealth as a cause of ruin generally rather than wealth gained by coveting another's goods.

178.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
178.explanation: Guru Nanak names kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing) as the true path, in place of living off what belongs to others.
178.tie_back: The Kural says one's wealth is kept from dwindling by not coveting what is in another's hands; Guru Nanak's answer is to live on one's own honest labour and share it.
178.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
178._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: honest earning is the positive form of not coveting, but the verse says nothing about wealth not diminishing, and the Kural's pun on ahkaamai and vehkaamai has no equivalent.

179.quote_or_event: “Maya is the slave of the Lord's devotees; it works for them.”
179.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that worldly wealth, which enslaves the grasping, comes to serve those who are devoted to God.
179.tie_back: The Kural says fortune seeks out, of her own accord, the wise who do not covet; Guru Amar Das says worldly wealth becomes the servant of the devoted.
179.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 231, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
179._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on wealth coming to serve the righteous; Sikhism does not personify fortune as the goddess Thiru, and the verse speaks of devotion rather than of not coveting.

180.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
180.explanation: In a salok in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir sets greed against forgiveness: one leads to spiritual death, the other is where God dwells.
180.tie_back: The Kural's closing antithesis says coveting gives birth to destruction while the strength of not wanting gives birth to victory; Kabir draws the same contrast between greed and death on one side and the divine presence on the other.
180.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir, Salok 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
180._accuracy_note: Strong fit for the first half (greed brings destruction); the other pole is forgiveness rather than the Kural's freedom from wanting, and Kabir is a bhagat whose hymns are Sikh scripture, not a Guru.
